t: What a Precision Magnetic Screwdriver Set Is
title: What a Precision Magnetic Screwdriver Set Is
description: A precision magnetic screwdriver set is a handle plus interchangeable bits covering the small fasteners in PCs and electronics — Phillips, flathead, hex, and Torx in tiny sizes — with magnetic bit retention so screws stay on the tip. PC chassis spaces are tight and screws are small; a precision set with the right bits turns stripped-screw frustration into smooth work. The iFixit Mako-style 64-bit kits are the popular benchmark.

demo.program:
bits = ["Phillips #000,#00,#0,#1,#2", "Torx T3-T10", "Hex 1.5-4mm",
        "Flathead 1.5-3mm", "Pentalobe", "Spudger/picks"]
print("Precision set coverage (64-bit kit style):")
for b in bits:
    print(f"  - {b}")
print("Magnetic retention: screws stay on the tip in tight chassis spaces.")

t: Bit Types Every PC Builder Actually Uses
title: Bit Types Every PC Builder Actually Uses
description: The bits that earn their keep: Phillips #2 for case and PSU screws, Phillips #1 for motherboard and drive screws, Phillips #0 for M.2 and small brackets, Torx T10/T15 for some GPU and cooler mounts, hex 2.5-3mm for water-cooling fittings, and flathead for prying (not screwing). Ninety percent of PC work is Phillips #1 and #2 — the rest of the kit exists for the other ten percent that stops a build cold without them.

demo.program:
use = [("Phillips #2", "case, PSU screws", "daily"),
       ("Phillips #1", "motherboard, drives", "daily"),
       ("Phillips #0", "M.2, small brackets", "weekly"),
       ("Torx T10/T15", "GPU/cooler mounts", "occasional"),
       ("Hex 2.5-3mm", "water fittings", "occasional")]
for bit, job, freq in use:
    print(f"  {bit:<14} {job:<22} {freq}")
print("90% of PC work: Phillips #1 + #2. The rest saves the other 10%.")

title: How Magnetic Bit Retention Works
description: The bit holder has a magnet that holds the bit, and the bit's own magnetism (or the holder's field extending through it) holds the screw on the tip. Good sets keep a screw on the tip through positioning; cheap sets drop it halfway to the hole. You can boost any bit by stroking it across a strong magnet. Demagnetize with reverse strokes when magnetism attracts metal filings into sensitive spots.

demo.program:
print("Chain: handle magnet -> holds bit -> field extends -> holds screw on tip.")
print("Good set: screw survives positioning. Cheap set: drops it halfway.")
print("Boost: stroke bit across strong magnet (one direction).")
print("Remove: reverse strokes (when filings stick where they shouldn't).")

t: Handle Design: What Makes a Driver Comfortable and Effective
title: Handle Design: What Makes a Driver Comfortable and Effective
description: A good precision handle has a knurled or textured grip that turns with fingertip pressure, a rotating end cap so you can press down while spinning with the other hand, and a slim profile that fits between GPU and side panel. Ratcheting handles speed long screw runs (case panels, radiators) but add bulk. For PC work, a slim spinner handle beats a bulky ratchet nine times in ten.

demo.program:
print("Good handle: textured grip + rotating end cap (press + spin) + slim profile.")
print("Ratchet: faster on long runs (panels, radiators), bulkier in tight spots.")
print("PC verdict: slim spinner handle wins 9/10. Ratchet for the 10th.")

t: Use Case: Motherboard Installation Without Stripping
title: Use Case: Motherboard Installation Without Stripping
description: Motherboard screws strip when the bit is wrong size, angled, or over-torqued. The method: Phillips #1 (not #2) for M3 board screws, driver perfectly vertical, press down firmly while turning slowly, and stop the instant the screw seats — board screws need snug, not crushed. The standoff threads are brass and soft; a stripped standoff means pliers and regret.

demo.program:
print("Board screws: Phillips #1, vertical, press + slow turn, stop at seat.")
print("Snug, NOT crushed: brass standoffs strip easily.")
print("Stripped standoff = pliers + regret. Right bit + vertical + stop = never.")

t: Use Case: M.2 Screws and Tiny Fasteners
title: Use Case: M.2 Screws and Tiny Fasteners
description: M.2 screws want Phillips #0 and a delicate touch — they thread into soft standoffs and snap if forced. Magnetize the bit so the tiny screw stays on the tip, position over the standoff, and turn with fingertip pressure only. If the screw resists, back it out and restart straight; cross-threading a 2 mm screw ruins the standoff. Never use a power driver on M.2 hardware.

demo.program:
print("M.2: Phillips #0, magnetized tip, fingertip pressure only.")
print("Resists? Back out, restart straight. Cross-threaded 2mm = ruined standoff.")
print("NEVER power drivers on M.2 hardware.")

t: Use Case: PSU and Case Screws at Torque
title: Use Case: PSU and Case Screws at Torque
description: Case and PSU screws (#6-32, Phillips #2) take real torque — this is where a full-size driver or ratchet earns its keep. Drive them firm but not gorilla-tight; over-torqued case screws strip the chassis threads and make the next teardown miserable. Thread each screw by hand two turns first to guarantee straight engagement, then drive it home.

demo.program:
print("Case/PSU (#6-32, P2): firm, not gorilla-tight.")
print("Hand-thread 2 turns first (guarantees straight engagement), then drive.")
print("Over-torque strips chassis threads: next teardown pays for it.")

title: Technique: The Vertical Press-and-Turn
description: Stripped Phillips heads come from angle plus spin without pressure. The press-and-turn: seat the bit fully in the screw head, align the driver dead vertical, press down with real force through the end cap, and turn slowly. The downward force keeps the bit seated; the slow turn keeps it from camming out. This one technique prevents more stripped screws than any tool upgrade.

demo.program:
print("Press-and-turn: seat bit fully -> dead vertical -> press hard -> turn SLOW.")
print("Down force keeps bit seated; slow turn prevents cam-out.")
print("Prevents more stripped screws than any tool upgrade.")

t: Bit Care: Cleaning, Demagnetizing, and Replacement
title: Bit Care: Cleaning, Demagnetizing, and Replacement
description: Wipe bits after use — metal dust in the case sticks to magnetic tips and then to your next screw. Demagnetize bits that collect filings near sensitive work. Replace bits the moment the tip shows wear: a worn Phillips #1 looks fine but cams out and strips heads. Bits are consumables; a 64-bit kit's most-used three bits deserve individual replacements, not a whole new kit.

demo.program:
print("Wipe bits after use (metal dust hitchhikes on magnetic tips).")
print("Demagnetize when filings collect near sensitive spots.")
print("Worn tip = cams out = strips heads. Bits are consumables: replace the worn ones.")

t: Power Drivers in PC Building: When They Help and Hurt
title: Power Drivers in PC Building: When They Help and Hurt
description: Electric precision screwdrivers speed panel and radiator screw runs enormously — but their torque strips small screws instantly. Rules: lowest torque setting, only on #6-32 and larger, never on motherboard/M.2/fan screws, and always hand-start threads first. A power driver is a bulk tool for panels; precision work stays manual. One stripped standoff costs more time than the driver ever saved.

demo.program:
print("Power driver rules: lowest torque, #6-32+ only, hand-start threads first.")
print("NEVER on motherboard / M.2 / fan screws.")
print("Bulk panels: yes. Precision: manual. One stripped standoff > all time saved.")

t: Precision Set vs Full-Size Drivers vs Multi-Tool
title: Precision Set vs Full-Size Drivers vs Multi-Tool
description: Precision sets win inside the case — slim, right bits, magnetic. Full-size drivers win on case exteriors and PSU screws where torque matters. Multi-tools win in the go-bag where space beats ergonomics. The bench wants the precision set as the primary and one full-size #2 for exteriors; the field kit gets the multi-tool. Right driver per context, not one driver for everything.

demo.program:
print("precision set: inside the case (slim, right bits, magnetic) - PRIMARY")
print("full-size #2   : exteriors, PSU screws (torque)")
print("multi-tool     : go-bag (space > ergonomics)")
print("Bench: precision set + one full-size #2. Field: multi-tool.")

t: Buying Guide: What Separates Good Sets From Junk
title: Buying Guide: What Separates Good Sets From Junk
description: Good sets have hardened S2 steel bits (not soft chrome-vanadium that rounds off), precise bit tolerances (a sloppy #1 strips like a wrong size), a real magnet in the holder, and a case that actually holds the bits (bits rattling loose are bits lost). Expect 20 to 35 dollars for a quality 64-bit kit. The 8-dollar kits have soft bits that become screw-strippers within months.

demo.program:
print("Good: S2 hardened bits, precise tolerances, real holder magnet, bits stay put.")
print("Junk: soft bits (round off), sloppy fit (strips like wrong size), loose case.")
print("$20-35: quality 64-bit kit. $8 kits become screw-strippers in months.")

title: Advanced: Working Around Stripped Screws
description: When a screw strips despite everything: try a larger bit pressed hard, a rubber band between bit and head for grip, or screw-extractor bits for the truly stuck. For stripped standoffs, grip with pliers from below while turning. Prevention beats extraction every time — but every builder eventually meets the screw that teaches them the press-and-turn.

demo.program:
print("Stripped? try: larger bit + hard press -> rubber band for grip -> extractor bits.")
print("Stripped standoff: pliers below + turn above.")
print("Prevention wins. But every builder meets the screw that teaches press-and-turn.")

title: Storage and Bit Inventory Discipline
description: A precision set is only useful if the bits are in it — the discipline is returning every bit to its labeled slot after each job and doing a slot check before the case closes. Missing-bit protocol: stop, find it (it is usually in the case), never leave a loose bit inside a PC. Photograph the full set once; the photo is the inventory reference for slot checks.

demo.program:
print("Discipline: every bit back to its labeled slot after each job.")
print("Slot check before case closes. Missing bit? STOP and find it (it's in the case).")
print("Photo the full set once: the inventory reference.")

title: The Complete Precision-Driver Discipline
description: The master discipline: right bit for the screw, press-and-turn always, hand-start every thread, torque matched to the fastener (fingertip for M.2, firm for #6-32), bits wiped and slotted after each job, worn bits replaced not tolerated, power drivers only on bulk panels. Screws are the most-handled part of any build — the driver discipline is the build discipline.

demo.program:
disc = ["right bit per screw", "press-and-turn always", "hand-start threads",
        "torque matched to fastener", "bits wiped + slotted after jobs",
        "worn bits replaced", "power drivers on bulk only"]
for i, d in enumerate(disc, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {d}")
print("Most-handled part of any build: driver discipline IS build discipline.")
